newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: SLOVAK PARLIAMENT WITHDRAWS CONTROVERSIAL LAW.
newsitem.headline: SLOVAK PARLIAMENT WITHDRAWS CONTROVERSIAL LAW.

text.p: Slovakia's ruling coalition late on Thursday withdrew a heavily-criticised law borrowing on communist-era anti-subversion legislation from parliament's agenda, but a revised law could reach the agenda by year's end.

Peter Brnak, Chairman of the Constitutional Committtee and member of the Movement for a Democratic Slovakia (HZDS), told parliament withdrawal of the law was "a result of the will of the coalition to draft better-quality legislation."

Jan Cuper, a leading HZDS deputy, told Reuters on Thursday HZDS was working on a new version of the law, originally drafted by junior coalition partner ultra-right nationalist Slovak National Party (SNS), as a price for supporting a treaty with neighbouring Hungary.
"A new version (of the law) will be probably be placed on the agenda of the December session of parliament."
The controversial penal code with "protection of the republic" legislation, was originally approved in March but later returned by President Michal Kovac to revision.
The United States and the European Union have criticised the law, an ammendment to the penal code, and other legislation drafted by the government of Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar.
Both have expressed concerns that Slovakia is foot-dragging on its commitment to democracy.

Under the law people could be punished for acts such as organising anti-government demonstrations or publishing "false information" abroad. Some of its wording is almost identical to anti-subversion laws scrapped after the 1989 fall of communism.

The opposition proposed the law be wiped off the agenda of the current parliament which comes up for re-election in the autumn of 1998, but the proposal was rejected by the three- party coalition which holds a majority in the legislative body.
